newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi bomb suspect denies being in country at time.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bomb suspect denies being in country at time.

text.p: A Saudi Arabian being held in Canada as a security risk on Monday denied he was involved in last June's bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. airmen and said he was not in the country at the time.

Speaking from behind heavy glass in an interview with a small group of reporters, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh said: "I was astonished to be accused, and especially to be accused of being the driver of the (get-away) car."

Soft-spoken, wearing silver-rimmed glasses and a dark blue prison uniform, Sayegh, 28, sat alone in a small room marked "Maximum Security Visits." His hair was neatly groomed and he had a beard that looked several days old.

Sayegh said that about two years ago he had fled Saudi Arabia to Syria, from where he proceeded to Ottawa last August -- two months after the bombing of a military housing complex in eastern Saudi Arabia -- and applied to be a refugee.
He said he had stamps in his passport to prove his whereabouts.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation wants to question him in connection with the bombing and U.S. officials in Washington said he was suspected of being the driver of a get-away car used after the bombing.
But he denied having a connection to any dissident or guerrilla organizations: "I have no relations with any organization. I have relations with the general public."

It became clear during the interview that he was a devout Shi'ite Muslim. He did religious studies in Qom, the main Shi'ite learning center in Iran, where the late revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini also studied.
He did not have a secular profession -- he had once worked as a clerk in a small store -- and in Syria he said he "sat around" during his self-imposed exile.
He said he feared going back to Saudi Arabia because of the way the Sunni Muslim rulers treated Shi'ites and said he would not cooperate with the FBI if it sought to question him.

Sayegh said he would be willing to go to Saudi Arabia, however, if he would be monitored by a human rights association and if there were a lawyer and a public hearing -- but he plainly did not believe this would be the case.
"Anything can happen, from beatings to killings," he said.
Asked his opinion of U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia, site of the sacred Muslim cities of Mecca and Medina, he smiled and declined comment.
But he said he had no fear of his treatment in Canada.
"I have no fear because I believe in Canadian law," he said through a translator, who sat with the reporters.
"I came to Canada because I know it's a democratic country, and because it respects human rights and because it receives refugees kindly."
Since arriving in Ottawa he had been living on welfare because Canadian law forbids refugee applicants from working, he said. He was arrested on Tuesday at a convenience store in Ottawa.
His wife, 5-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son are under house arrest in Qatif in Saudi Arabia, he added.
